source.title: VGGT-$\Omega$
source.authors: Jian-Yuan Wang; Ming-Hao Chen; Shang-Zhan Zhang; Nikita Karaev; Johannes L. Schonberger; Patrick Labatut; Piotr Bojanowski; David Novotný; Andrea Vedaldi; Christian Rupprecht

record.file_problem: None; the full paper and supplementary material are present.
record.tranche_reason: It extends model- and data-scaling measurements to feed-forward 3D reconstruction models, using point error rather than language-model cross-entropy.
record.gate_note: The study reports reconstruction point-error outcomes for model-size and data-size sweeps, and for register-attention architecture variants. Benchmark results for other reconstruction methods, language alignment, and VLA performance do not test the scaling versions.
record.test_reason: The study sweeps model size (0.2B–10B) and training-data size (about 2K–2M sequences) for a feed-forward 3D reconstruction transformer. It reports held-out point error falling monotonically, which bears on V5 in a new modality. It fits no power law and measures no language-model loss.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors state that VGGT-Ω 'scales predictably with model capacity and data size' and hedge that curve shapes suggest power laws 'might' characterize scaling. They fit no law.
record.recipe_differences: The study scales visual 3D reconstruction models and measures point error, rather than language-model parameter, token, and compute scaling using held-out cross-entropy.
record.method_sensitivity: The reconstruction result differs with the proportion of global-attention layers replaced by register attention: replacing 25% has nearly identical performance, while replacing all causes a considerable drop.

fits_no_version.finding: Replacing 25% of global-attention layers with register attention leaves point error nearly unchanged (0.071 vs 0.073). Replacing all of them drops performance to original-VGGT level while cutting FLOPs to 6%.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In multi-view vision transformers, most cross-frame global attention can be replaced by register-mediated attention with little accuracy loss, up to a point.

record.problems: Scaling results use reconstruction point error rather than held-out pretraining loss; no fitted exponents, compute-optimal allocation, or uncertainty estimates are reported. The model-size sweep is presented graphically without individual size-to-value assignments in the text.
record.rows_left_out: No additional results bearing on the tested versions were left out. Other benchmark, application, and training-ablation results do not test these claim versions.

untested.parts: No language models or pretraining cross-entropy.
No small-run fits used to predict larger runs.
No fixed-compute allocation between parameters and data.
No depth/width sweep at fixed parameter count for language models; the register-attention ablations are a different kind of architecture change in a vision model.
No fitted power-law form or exponents. No repeated-data, fine-tuning or transfer scaling. Only one vision task (3D reconstruction), with point error rather than training loss.
No relation of downstream task performance to pretraining loss or scale across a sweep.
No exponents, fitting choices, or curve bending analysed.

missing.what: Ours-1B vs Ours-10B on six benchmarks. The 10B model beats 1B on every camera AUC and depth metric, e.g. Sintel AUC@3° 35.5→40.0 and δ1.25 89.9→93.5.
Intermediate point-error values of the model- and data-size sweeps, plus the per-size architecture (blocks and hidden sizes differ across sizes).

record.verdict_notes: Tranche T3: a new modality with a non-loss metric (point error). The reader's V4 links were dropped: a register-attention ablation in a vision model is not the LM depth/width shape claim. Confounds for V5: tokens are held roughly fixed across both sweeps, and model sizes change both depth and width. The 10B model therefore may be data-limited, and the data sweep mixes in repetition.

versions.untested_parts: No language models or held-out pretraining cross-entropy are measured.
No fits from small runs are used to predict the losses of larger runs.
No fixed-compute allocation sweep or compute-optimal parameter/token trend is measured.
Tests register-attention proportions only; it does not sweep depth, width, or a broad range of architecture details.
Tests model and data scaling for feed-forward 3D reconstruction using point error, not other vision tasks, modalities, repeated data, or fine-tuning and transfer regimes.
No downstream-task performance is related predictably to reconstruction pretraining loss or scale.
No scaling exponents, compute-optimal split, fitting choices, or systematic curve departures are analyzed.

rows.subject: VGGT-Ω model-size sweep
rows.operation_detail: Increased model capacity and measured reconstruction point error.

conditions.value: approximately the same number for all models

rows.note: The text says reconstruction accuracy improves consistently with model capacity and that the curve suggests power-law-like scaling. The figure shows point-error values, but this row records the sweep as a whole rather than assigning plotted values to individual sizes.
rows.check: Values are readable from Fig. 1(a): 0.107, 0.073, 0.057, 0.046 across the four sizes. Baseline should be 0.107 and value 0.046, not 'figure only'. The size-to-value mapping is not stated in text. Width and depth also change across sizes (12/12/24/16 blocks). Tokens are held roughly fixed, so data may become the bottleneck at 10B. No power law is fitted.

source_check.correct: state=cannot_determine for V5: monotonic improvement and a suggested power-law-like shape do not establish the same power-law form. Retain figure-only endpoint reporting; the extracted figure does not reliably pair every parameter count with an error.
source_check.locator_found: Figure 1(a) and caption; Section 4.3, Model and data size
source_check.problem: Observed overstates evidence for V5's power-law-form claim.

rows.subject: VGGT-Ω data-size sweep
rows.operation_detail: Increased the number of training sequences and measured reconstruction point error.

conditions.value: few thousand to 2 million, increased in 10× steps

rows.note: The authors state that point error drops monotonically from 0.275 to 0.073 as training sequences increase in 10× steps; they describe the curves as suggesting power laws.
rows.check: Intermediate values 0.210, 0.160 and 0.129 are also given in Fig. 1(b). Training tokens are held roughly constant, so smaller-data runs repeat sequences; this is a unique-data sweep, not a token sweep. The authors only say power laws 'might characterize' the curves; no fit or exponent is given.

relationships.condition: Feed-forward 3D reconstruction, model sweep 0.2B–10B and unique-data sweep about 2K–2M sequences, at fixed tokens
relationships.reason: Point error falls monotonically: 0.107→0.046 with model size (r1) and 0.275→0.073 with data (r2). The authors call the curves power-law-like but fit no law, so support is for monotone scaling only.
relationships.display_finding: Point error decreased from 0.107 to 0.046 with model size and from 0.275 to 0.073 with data; the curves were described as power-law-like without fitting that form.

relation.reason: The study directly varies scale and measures reconstruction error, providing relevant evidence for beyond-text scaling, although its functional form remains undetermined.
